text: Anil Biswas (2 March 1944 – 26 March 2006), commonly known as Keru, was an Indian communist politician who served as the secretary of the West Bengal State Committee of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and as a member of the party's politburo from 1998 until his death in 2006. Born into a middle-class Mahishya family in Darermath village near Karimpur, Nadia district, to Ashutosh Biswas and Prafulla Kumari Debi, he lost his father at a young age. While in high school, he became interested in the Left movement and joined Krishnagar Government College in 1961, where he was influenced by Marxist leaders Harinarayan Adhikari and Dinesh Majumdar and became an active member of the Students' Federation of India, serving as a student leader in college elections. After completing an Honours degree in Political Science, he moved to Kolkata for further studies. He became a full-fledged member of the CPI(M) in 1965 and was arrested under the Defence of India Rules 1962, spending 11 months in prison, during which he completed his master's degree in political science. In 1969, he became a whole-time party member and began his party work as a journalist with Ganashakti, the party's daily newspaper. He was elected to the CPIM West Bengal state committee in 1978 and to the state secretariat in 1982. He edited Ganashakti between 1983 and 1998, during which the newspaper achieved its peak circulation. In 1985, he was elected to the party's Central Committee. In 1998, he joined the politburo, mentored by Pramod Dasgupta, and took over as secretary of the West Bengal State Committee after his predecessor Sailen Dasgupta resigned due to ill-health and old age. He was reelected as state secretary in 2002 and 2005. He also served as editor of Marxbadi Path (The Road of the Marxist), the theoretical quarterly in West Bengal. Known for his strategic acumen, he played a key role in the party's political decisions, including the decision to appoint Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee as Chief Minister of West Bengal in place of Jyoti Basu before the 2000 West Bengal Legislative Assembly Elections—a move that addressed public frustration with over two decades of the same chief minister and led to a major victory for the Left Front despite strong opposition from Mamata Banerjee's TMC. His effective management of media and ground workers during the 2006 West Bengal Assembly Election significantly reduced the opposition's seat count, as he had a deep understanding of public sentiment both in the media and on the ground. It is widely believed that the deaths of Anil Biswas and other key ground leaders like Subhas Chakraborty created opportunities for the opposition to come to power and replace the Left Front. He died on 26 March 2006 after being hospitalized due to a brain haemorrhage on 18 March. According to his last wishes, his body was donated to NRS Medical College and Hospital. He is survived by his wife Gita and daughter Ajanta.
